nameStory: Ground-ivy gets its name from its ivy-like habit of creeping along the ground, though it's not related to true ivy at all! Its many colorful nicknames tell stories of old uses - 'gill-over-the-ground' and 'alehoof' hint at its historical role in brewing beer before hops became popular, while 'creeping charlie' and 'run-away-robin' capture its enthusiastic spreading nature.
description: Ground-ivy is a low-growing, evergreen creeper that forms dense mats across the forest floor and lawns. This aromatic member of the mint family spreads by trailing stems that root as they go, creating carpets of rounded, scalloped leaves. The plant stays close to the ground, rarely rising more than a few inches tall, but can spread several feet in all directions. In spring, it produces small purple-blue flowers that stand upright above the leafy mat.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Round to kidney-shaped leaves with scalloped edges, arranged in opposite pairs along square stems - crush one and smell the strong, minty aroma that's unmistakable

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, carpet-like mats by sending out trailing runners that root at every joint where they touch soil, creating an interconnected network

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small purple-blue flowers with white markings appear in clusters along upright stems in spring, each flower having the typical mint family two-lipped shape

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square stems that feel distinctly four-sided when rolled between your fingers - a classic mint family trait that you can feel even on the thin trailing runners

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Leaves feel slightly fuzzy and soft to the touch, with a fresh, somewhat oily texture that releases fragrance when handled

habitat: Ground-ivy thrives in partially shaded areas with moist, rich soil, making it common in woodlands, woodland edges, and shaded lawns throughout New England. You'll often find it carpeting areas under trees, along trails, and in disturbed forest areas where it can outcompete native plants. It's particularly abundant in suburban areas where it escapes from lawns into adjacent natural areas.

seasonality.spring: Purple-blue flowers appear in April and May, standing upright above the mat of leaves like tiny beacons - this is the easiest time to spot it from a distance.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade and the plant focuses on vegetative growth, spreading rapidly through its runner system and maintaining its dense green carpet.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may take on slight purplish tints but remain green and recognizable, continuing to spread and establish new root systems.
seasonality.winter: Stays evergreen under snow, maintaining its mat of rounded leaves - often one of the few green things you'll see when snow melts in protected spots.

funFact: Ground-ivy was so valued by early European settlers that they intentionally brought it to America as a medicine and brewing ingredient - but it loved its new home so much that it's now considered one of New England's most persistent invasive plants, nearly impossible to remove once established due to its extensive underground network!
confusionNotes: Often confused with creeping jenny (Lysimachia nummularia), but ground-ivy has scalloped leaf edges and square stems while creeping jenny has smooth, round leaf edges and round stems. Remember: scalloped edges and square stems = ground-ivy; smooth and round = creeping jenny.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this with creeping jenny - that name is sometimes used for ground-ivy but more properly belongs to Lysimachia nummularia, a completely different plant in the primrose family. Ground-ivy is considered an aggressive invasive species in New England, despite its historical importance as a medicinal and brewing herb.
compareHints: Ground-ivy is the only member of its genus in New England, making it unique among our flora. Compared to other mint family members like wild mint or self-heal, ground-ivy is distinguished by its prostrate, mat-forming growth habit and kidney-shaped leaves with pronounced scalloped edges. Most other mints grow upright and have more pointed, toothed leaves rather than the rounded, scalloped ones of ground-ivy.
